title: How to Merge Two Customer Feedback Programs After an Acquisition or Reorg
summary: Merging two feedback programs after an acquisition is a sequencing problem. Five steps: pick the base code frame, grade metrics, share one theme set.
body_markdown:
Two companies become one. Each arrives with its own survey, its own[code frame](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-build-a-customer-feedback-taxonomy) , and an executive who already trusts a number. Somebody now has to produce one answer to "how are customers doing?" before the first post-close board pack.


The merge isn't a data-migration job. It's four decisions: which code frame becomes the base, which metrics can still be trended, what you standardize first, and who owns the result. Thematic's part is narrow but load-bearing. A Lens combines both programs' datasets and analyzes them together under a single, unified set of themes, which is the only way two sources genuinely share one taxonomy instead of two copies of one.


## The five-step process


1. **Pick the base code frame before anyone logs in.** Decide whose taxonomy survives, or whether neither does, as a documented decision rather than a default.
2. **Grade every metric for whether it can still be trended.** Green, yellow or red, before you promise anyone a trend line.
3. **Put both sources under one theme set, not two copies of one.** Copies drift. A shared theme set does not.
4. **Standardize in a sequence.** Fix the instrument going forward first. Reconcile history second, and only as far back as you need it.
5. **Name one owner, and declare the breaks.** One person approves structural edits, and you say which trend lines did not survive.


## Step 1: Pick the base code frame before anyone logs in


The first decision is whose taxonomy becomes the base, and the default answer is usually wrong.


Acquirers tend to assume theirs wins because it's theirs. What matters is which program is better, not which is senior.[Gallup found](https://news.gallup.com/businessjournal/183443/bank-mergers-may-chase-away-customers.aspx) that customers of acquired banks leave at 8% against a 5% industry average. Attrition at the target rises to about 10% when the acquirer is less engaged with its customers than the target was, and falls to 6% when the acquirer is more engaged. Inheriting the weaker program costs real customers.


Expect a structural collision. One side's code frame is usually shaped around products and the other[around the customer journey](https://getthematic.com/insights/feedback-taxonomy-product-vs-journey) , a real design decision whose answer depends on your program rather than on who signed the deal. Thematic's taxonomy is two levels deep, base themes and sub-themes, so a three-level legacy frame has to collapse into two whatever you decide.


Then test the result for reliability, not tidiness.[Content analysis has a standard](https://www.asc.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/2021-03/Answering%20the%20Call%20for%20a%20Standard%20Reliability%20Measure%20for%20Coding%20Data.pdf) for this: whether a coding instrument, serving as common instructions to different observers, yields the same data from each of them. Have an analyst from each side independently code the same 50 comments against the merged frame. Where they disagree, the frame is ambiguous, and executive sign-off won't fix that.


## Step 2: Grade every metric for whether it can still be trended


Don't declare the combined history comparable, and don't declare it dead. Grade it item by item.


Pew Research Center[did exactly this](https://www.pewresearch.org/2025/02/26/appendix-a-comparing-results-across-religious-landscape-studies/) when it changed how it measured. It ran a parallel telephone bridge study of 1,519 US adults purely to test which questions survived the change, then color-coded every question. Green questions "produce results in the new survey that can safely be compared" with the earlier studies. Yellow questions "appear to be subject to modest mode effects, but they nevertheless can be cautiously compared." Red questions "cannot be compared with the previous studies." The reason for grading rather than ruling: "not all questions are equally subject to these 'mode effects.'"


A[mode effect](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/02/27/what-our-transition-to-online-polling-means-for-decades-of-phone-survey-trends/) is the difference in a result that comes from how you asked rather than from what changed. In one Pew experiment, 62% of phone respondents gave an answer that only 48% of online respondents gave to the identical question. A 14-point gap, no change in opinion.


Two merging programs almost never asked the same question the same way. Take the metrics each side reports upward, grade each one, and put the grade in writing before anyone builds a slide on it.


## Step 3: Put both sources under one theme set, not two copies of one


This is the step teams get wrong, because the wrong version looks identical for about a quarter.


In Thematic, a theme structure cannot be shared between datasets. You can copy one: the Themes Editor's Import themes option copies an existing dataset's themes into another, and themes can be copied and pasted between Lenses and existing datasets. But a copy is an independent structure from the moment it lands. Each side edits its own, and the two drift apart quietly while everyone believes they're on one taxonomy.


A Lens is what actually shares. It combines one or more datasets and analyzes them together under a single, unified set of themes. A new data source added to an existing Lens automatically picks up that Lens's themes. Plan for up to ten datasets per Lens, and expect initial theme generation to take a few hours.


Two settings matter for a merge. **Weighting:** by default every response in a Lens carries the same weight, so a program with 50,000 responses drowns out one with 500. Dataset weighting sets a ratio per source, and the ratios need not add up to 100 because only their relationship matters. **Scores:** if the two programs ran different metrics, a Lens score maps one number column from each dataset onto a common range, so net promoter score (NPS), customer satisfaction (CSAT) and a five-star rating roll into[one comparable number](https://getthematic.com/insights/standardize-cx-metric-across-brands-channels) .


This scales further than it sounds. One national wholesale broadband provider arrived with eight data sources telling eight different stories, and ended up with more than 100 themes across two levels of detail.


## Step 4: Standardize in a sequence, not all at once


Social science has a name for the two halves of this job, and CX teams almost never use it.


**[Ex-ante harmonization](https://www.cessda.eu/Training-Resources/Resource-crd-2616)** means making data comparable by designing it that way from the start: one instrument, one code frame, one set of definitions for everything collected from now on. **Ex-post harmonization** means making already-collected data comparable after the fact. The first is cheap. The second is the expensive half, and it gets harder the further back you reach.


So sequence them. Agree the forward-looking instrument in the first weeks, because every day you wait adds more unharmonized data to the pile. Then reconcile history only as far back as someone will actually use it. For that history, code a sample of comments under both programs' categories to see where they line up, and restate only the periods someone will report on.


Know what re-applying themes does. Thematic re-analyzes existing feedback under the new taxonomy rather than applying it only to new data, so older and newer data sit on the same themes list and you can still[trend across the change](https://getthematic.com/insights/keep-feedback-trend-lines-comparable) . The flip side: numbers you've already reported will move. Say so before it happens, not after.


The discipline is rare:[BCG found](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2015/why-deals-fail.aspx) fewer than 40% of corporate leaders have a standardized approach to post-merger integration at all.


## Step 5: Name one owner, and declare the breaks


Two programs merging produces two people who each believe they[own the taxonomy](https://getthematic.com/insights/who-owns-feedback-themes-taxonomy) , which in practice means nobody does. And if the reorg means one of them leaves, plan for[what happens when the person who built a feedback program leaves](https://getthematic.com/insights/feedback-program-owner-leaves) before they go.


Assign the decision explicitly. The clearest published framing separates five roles, and a merged program needs a name against each:


- **Recommend.** Who drafts the proposed structure.
- **Agree.** Who holds narrow, predefined veto rights.
- **Perform.** Who does the work.
- **Input.** Who supplies facts and views, with no veto.
- **Decide.** The one person who makes the call and commits the organization.


There's a product reason to keep structural edits with one person: applying themes locks the structure for all editors, and simultaneous edits can race. Batch the merge as one set of changes under one owner. Thematic's Themes Editor auto-saves edits to a draft and changes nothing until someone clicks Apply themes. Revert Draft rolls back to any of the last three applied versions, showing who applied each one and when. That's a safety net, not a version history.


Then say which trend lines died. Pew's practice when a measurement change breaks a series is to choose openly between breaking the trend, connecting it with a visible flag, or connecting it with less emphasis once several years of evidence accumulate. Any of the three is defensible. Silently splicing two differently-measured histories into one line is not.


Tell customers too. In[J.D. Power research](http://images.dealer.com/jdpa/pdf/09-US-MergersAcquisitions-SR.pdf) on bank mergers, the satisfaction gap between customers who got prior notice of a change and those who did not was 119 index points on a 1,000-point scale.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Freezing the feedback program during integration.** Common, and backwards. Integration is the period of highest churn risk, which is when the signal is worth most.
- **Defaulting to the acquirer's taxonomy because it is the acquirer's.** Pick the better frame, or build a third.
- **Copying a taxonomy when you meant to share one.** Two copies look like agreement and behave like divergence.
- **Promising an unbroken trend line.** Grade the metrics first, then promise only the green ones.
- **Quoting the "70 to 90% of mergers fail" statistic.** It traces to[one sentence in a 2011 HBR article](https://hbr.org/2011/03/the-big-idea-the-new-ma-playbook) that names no studies, no sample and no definition of failure. If you need a real number, BCG found 47% of deals produce a positive relative total shareholder return one year on.


## The short answer


Merging two customer feedback programs is a sequencing problem, not a migration problem. Pick the base code frame deliberately, grade every metric green, yellow or red before promising a trend, put both sources under one shared theme set rather than two copies, fix the forward-looking instrument before reconciling history, and give one named person the decision. Thematic's Lens is what makes the shared theme set real, with weighting so the larger program does not drown out the smaller one.


The test to run this week: take the ten themes each program reports on most, and check how many mean the same thing on both sides. The ones that do not are your merge.
